The Story of Sagardatt

I bow to Lord Jina and write this story so that readers may turn their minds away from sinful deeds.

In Kaushambi, there ruled a king named Jaipal. In his time lived a wealthy merchant named Samudradatta, whose wife was Samudradatta. They had a beautiful son named Sagardatt, so lovely that everyone longed to play with him. Their neighbor was a man named Gopayan, who through the ripening of past sins had fallen into poverty, and his greed for wealth had made him vicious. His wife was Seema, and their son was Somak, who was growing up and delighting his parents with his sweet, lisping speech.

One day, Sagardatt and Somak were playing together at Gopayan's house. Sagardatt was wearing jewelry at the time. The wicked Gopayan came upon them, and seeing the child adorned with gold, sinful desire arose in his heart. He shut the door and, under some pretense of reward, lured Sagardatt inside, with Somak running after them. Once inside, the cruel Gopayan slit the innocent child's throat with a knife, stripped him of all his ornaments, and buried the body in a pit.

For many days Sagardatt's parents searched for their child in vain. They concluded that some wicked person had killed him for his gold. The grief they suffered at the loss of their beloved son can only be understood by those who have endured such a fate. Helpless, they could only endure their sorrow.

Some days later, Somak was playing in Samudradatta's courtyard. Samudradatta's wife, moved by some impulse, called the boy lovingly and asked, "Dear child, tell me — where has your companion Sagardatt gone? Have you seen him?" Somak was a child, and with a child's pure heart, he blurted out that Sagardatt was buried in a pit inside his house. Upon hearing of her child's fate, the poor mother collapsed to the ground. Soon the news spread, the body was recovered, and Gopayan was brought to justice.

This story teaches that sinful deeds, no matter how well concealed, are eventually revealed. The innocence of a child exposed the murderer's guilt. As the saying goes: truth always comes to light, and the wicked cannot escape the consequences of their crimes.
